Australia is the driest inhabited continent. To understand its plants, follow the rain.
At the red centre, less than two hundred and fifty millimetres falls in a year.
Spinifex curls into spiky hummocks. They cover about a fifth of the land.
A little more rain, and the acacias arrive. Mulga tilts its branches upward, funnelling every drop down to its roots.
Then come the eucalypts. More than eight hundred species, making up three quarters of Australia's forests.
Fire is part of the rhythm here.
Within weeks, blackened trunks sprout again, from buds hidden deep beneath the bark.
In the wet mountains, mountain ash, one of the tallest flowering plants on Earth, reaches for a hundred metres.
And where the rain barely stops: rainforest. Layer upon layer, on less than one percent of the land.
But this walk, from desert to rainforest, is also a walk back in time.
Fifty million years ago, rainforest spread across much of Australia.
As the continent drifted north and dried, the green retreated to the edges, and tough, fire-ready bush claimed the heart.
Dry at the heart. Green at the edge. And still changing.
